Problem 1: Rotating system

A motor is fixed in a vertical position. One end of a rod of length $l$ and of negligible cross-section is attached to the lower end of the motor shaft by a pivot, so that the rod can rotate about the horizontal axis $o$ (Fig. 1). The rotor of the motor starts to rotate together with the axis $o$, and its angular velocity increases very slowly.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/czech-2006-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1

a) Explain why, in a real device, the rod deflects from the vertical position once a certain critical angular velocity $\omega_0$ is exceeded.

b) Determine how the deflection of the revolving rod from the vertical depends on the angular velocity of the rotor.

c) Construct the graph of this dependence if $l = 0.50\,\mathrm{m}$. At what angular velocity does the deflection of the rod from the vertical reach $60^\circ$?

Use the gravitational acceleration $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$. Neglect the effect of the surrounding air.

problems.title: Problem 2: Satellite

Problem 2: Satellite

An Earth satellite of mass $m = 150\,\mathrm{kg}$ was placed on a circular orbit of radius $R = 6.70\cdot10^{3}\,\mathrm{km}$.

a) What are its speed and its orbital period?

b) What is the total mechanical energy of the satellite? (The potential energy at infinite distance is taken as zero.)

c) How do the radius of the trajectory and the speed of the satellite change during one revolution if the upper layers of the atmosphere act on it with a drag force of magnitude $F = 7.50\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}$?

Solve the problem first in general, then for the given numerical values. Mass of the Earth $M = 5.98\cdot10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$, gravitational constant $\varkappa = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2\cdot kg^{-2}}$.

Problem 3: Periodic recharging of a capacitor

An electric circuit consists of a source of rectangular pulses, a switch, two resistors of resistances $r$ and $R$, and a capacitor of capacitance $C$ (Fig. 2). The rectangular pulses have amplitude $U_0$, duration $\tau$ and period $T$ (Fig. 3). The internal resistance of the source is negligible. (Among other things, this means that when the terminal voltage of the source is zero, the source behaves as a short circuit.)

When the switch is closed, after a long time the voltage across the capacitor will fluctuate about a constant mean value $U_C$, while the ripple $\Delta U$, i.e. the difference between the largest and the smallest value of the instantaneous voltage across the capacitor during one period of the source, will be much smaller than the mean value $U_C$.

a) Under the given assumptions, determine $U_C$ and $\Delta U$.

b) Determine the condition that the quantities $R$, $r$, $C$, $\tau$ and $T$ must satisfy for the assumption of the problem that $\Delta U \ll U_C$ to be ensured.

c) Verify that this condition is satisfied if $R = 1.00\,\mathrm{M\Omega}$, $r = 220\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, $C = 1.00\,\mathrm{\mu F}$, $\tau = 2.0\,\mathrm{ms}$, $T = 10.0\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $U_0 = 5.00\,\mathrm{V}$. Then calculate the numerical values of $U_C$ and $\Delta U$.

problems.title: Problem 1: Potential

Problem 1: Potential

Two point masses located in vacuum at a mutual distance $r$ carry negative electric charges $Q$ and $nQ$, where $n > 1$.

a) Determine the point of maximum electric potential on the line segment joining the two point masses, and the value of the potential there.

b) An electron is placed at this point and is slightly displaced off the line joining the two point masses. Determine the limiting speed of the electron at a very large distance. Carry out the solution both classically and relativistically.

problems.title: Problem 2: Binary star
problems.problem:
Problem 2: Binary star

Algol (beta Persei) is an eclipsing binary star whose two components revolve about their common centre of mass on approximately circular trajectories with period $T = 2.867$ days. The speeds of the two components have magnitudes $v_1 = 44.5\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and $v_2 = 203\,\mathrm{km/s}$.

a) Determine the radii of their trajectories and express them in astronomical units ($1\,\mathrm{AU} = 1.50\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{km}$).

b) Determine the masses of the two components and compare them with the mass of the Sun ($m_\odot = 1.99\cdot10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$).

c) Determine the magnitude of the gravitational forces with which the two components act on each other.

d) The values $v_1$, $v_2$ were calculated from the results of spectroscopic measurements. It was also found that the radial velocity with which the centre of mass of Algol recedes from the Sun has magnitude $v_c = 3.7\,\mathrm{km/s}$. Within what range does the wavelength of a spectral line of potassium in the spectrum of the less massive component of Algol vary during long-term observation, if in the spectrum of potassium from a terrestrial source we measure the value $\lambda_0 = 766.491\,\mathrm{nm}$? Consider the motion of the Earth around the Sun to be uniform with speed of magnitude $v_z = 30\,\mathrm{km/s}$; the line joining the Sun and Algol is inclined at the angle $\beta = 11.5^\circ$ to the plane of the ecliptic.

The gravitational constant is $\varkappa = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2\cdot kg^{-2}}$.

problems.title: Problem 3: Solar photon radiation
problems.problem:
Problem 3: Solar photon radiation

The solar radiation falling perpendicularly on $1\,\mathrm{m^2}$ of a plane surface in free space at a distance of $1\,\mathrm{AU}$ from the centre of the Sun has a power of $1365\,\mathrm{W}$. The Sun can be considered a perfectly black body, which absorbs all electromagnetic radiation falling on it and emits only its own radiation. According to the Stefan–Boltzmann law, the radiant exitance (i.e. the energy of the radiation leaving $1\,\mathrm{m^2}$ of the surface of the body in $1\,\mathrm{s}$) of such a body whose surface temperature is $T$ is

$$H = \sigma T^4, \qquad \text{where} \quad \sigma = 5.67\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\cdot m^{-2}\cdot K^{-4}}.$$

An observer on the surface of the Earth sees the diameter of the solar photosphere at an angle of $32'$; the radius of the Earth is $6371\,\mathrm{km}$, $1\,\mathrm{AU} = 149.6\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{km}$.

a) Determine the total radiant power (luminosity) $L$ of the Sun.

b) Determine the temperature $T_\mathrm{s}$ of the solar photosphere.

c) Determine the energy income of the solar radiation falling on the Earth in one day and in one year ($365.25$ days).

d) At present there is talk of a project in which a power plant made of solar cells would be installed in the Sahara: let us assume that $40\,\%$ of the radiation that has reached the upper boundary of the atmosphere falls on the surface of the Earth after passing through the atmosphere. We further assume that existing solar cells have an efficiency of $12\,\%$. How large a maximum power $P_\mathrm{max}$ would solar cells with an area of $1\,\mathrm{km^2}$ have?

e) A spherical satellite is launched into an orbit around the Earth so that it is continuously illuminated by the Sun. The satellite will have good thermal conductivity and its coating will have properties close to those of the surface of a perfectly black body. Determine its temperature $T_\mathrm{z}$. Neglect the radiation of the Earth falling on the satellite.

f) Determine the temperature $T_\mathrm{m}$ of the same satellite orbiting around Mars, if the mean distance of Mars from the Sun is $1.52\,\mathrm{AU}$.

g) Within what limits does the temperature of the satellites of the Earth and of Mars from parts e) and f) vary, if the numerical eccentricities of the trajectories of the two planets are $\varepsilon_\mathrm{z} = 0.017$ and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{m} = 0.093$, respectively?

The rods have a circular cross-section of area $S = 25.0\,\mathrm{mm^2}$, and after they were connected to the beam and to the ceiling, the stress in them was zero. After the assembly was completed, the supports were removed.

a) Assuming that the beam, the wall and the ceiling are perfectly rigid, determine the forces $\boldsymbol{F}_1$, $\boldsymbol{F}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{F}_0$ with which the rods and the wall acted on the beam, the elongations $\Delta l_1$, $\Delta l_2$ of the two rods, the stresses $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ in the rods, and the deviation $\varphi$ of the beam from the horizontal position.

b) During operation of the device the temperature of the rods rose to $t_2 = 35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while the temperature of the wall and the ceiling and their dimensions did not change. How did the values of the quantities calculated in part a) change?

c) At what temperature $t_3$ in both rods was the stress in rod 1 zero?

problems.title: Problem 1: Motions in the planetary system
problems.problem:
Problem 1: Motions in the planetary system

(a problem for the International Year of Astronomy)

On the basis of measurements made from the surface of the Earth, astronomers found that the (sidereal) orbital period of the planet Mars is $T_\mathrm{M} = 1.881$ years. The trajectory of the Earth can be considered a circle (the distance of the Earth from the Sun is $r_\mathrm{Z} = 1.000\,\mathrm{AU}$), but the trajectory of Mars is elliptical with numerical eccentricity $0.0934$. Both trajectories lie approximately in the same plane.

a) From the given data determine the length of the semi-major axis $a$ and of the semi-minor axis $b$ of the trajectory of Mars, the distance $r_\mathrm{a}$ of Mars from the Sun at aphelion and the distance $r_\mathrm{p}$ at perihelion.

b) Determine the areal velocity $w$ of Mars (i.e. the area swept by its radius vector per unit time), the magnitude $v_\mathrm{a}$ of its velocity at aphelion and the magnitude $v_\mathrm{p}$ of its velocity at perihelion. How does the ratio of the values $v_\mathrm{p}$, $v_\mathrm{a}$ depend on the numerical eccentricity of the trajectory of Mars?

c) Determine the values $k_\mathrm{sa}$, $k_\mathrm{sp}$ of the solar constant in the vicinity of Mars at its passages through aphelion and perihelion, if the solar constant in the vicinity of the Earth is $k_\mathrm{sZ} = 1\,360\,\mathrm{W\cdot m^{-2}}$. How does the ratio of the values $k_\mathrm{sp}$, $k_\mathrm{sa}$ depend on the numerical eccentricity of the trajectory of Mars?

d) For a journey from the vicinity of the Earth to the vicinity of Mars, the energetically optimal motion is along a trajectory in the shape of an ellipse that touches the trajectory of the Earth from outside and the trajectory of Mars from inside. Sketch the situation. What would be the time of motion of the spacecraft from the vicinity of the Earth to the vicinity of Mars if at the moment of approach Mars were 1) at perihelion, 2) at aphelion?

In the solution take $1\,\mathrm{AU} = 1.496\cdot10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, $1\ \text{year} = T_\mathrm{Z} = 3.156\cdot10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$. In the result choose a "reasonable" number of significant figures.

b) We remove the rod connecting the ends of the springs and divide all the shot into two bags of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$; we hang the first on the spring of stiffness $k_1$ and the second on the spring of stiffness $k_2$. What must the ratio $p = m_1/m_2$ be so that the extensions of both springs are equal?

c) Derive a relation for the total elastic energy of both springs as a function of the ratio $p$. Determine for which value of $p$ this energy is minimal and for which it is maximal. Calculate its values.

Problem 2: Particle in an electric field

Each of four point masses located at the vertices of a square of side length $a$ in vacuum has an electric charge $Q$ of the same sign.

a) Consider the $x$ axis identical with the axis of symmetry of the square perpendicular to the plane of the square, with its origin at the centre of the square. Problem 2: The Cassini–Huygens probe

On 14 January 2005 the Huygens module, carried by the Cassini probe, landed on Saturn's moon Titan. The moon Titan has radius $R_{\mathrm{T}}=2\,576\,\mathrm{km}$ and mass $M_{\mathrm{T}}=1.345\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{kg}$. Neglect the ellipticity of Titan's trajectory and assume that Titan moves on a circular orbit of radius $r_{\mathrm{T}}=1.22\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{km}$ with orbital period $T_{\mathrm{T}}=15.9$ days.

a) The time between two successive oppositions of Saturn is $T_{\mathrm{syn}}=378.1$ days. Determine the sidereal orbital period of Saturn $T_{\mathrm{sid}}$ and the length $a_{\mathrm{Sat}}$ of the semi-major axis of its elliptical trajectory. Determine the distances of Saturn from the Sun $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ at perihelion and $r_{\mathrm{a}}$ at aphelion of its trajectory, if the numerical eccentricity of its trajectory is $\varepsilon=0.056$.

b) What was the speed $v_{\mathrm{a}}$ of the probe on arrival at Saturn, if you know that Saturn was at aphelion? The Hohmann trajectory has the shape of half of an ellipse which at its initial point touches the trajectory of the Earth and at its final point the trajectory of Saturn, these points lying on opposite sides of the Sun.

c) During the landing of the Huygens module on the surface of Titan, the module was at a certain moment receding from the Cassini probe with speed $v=6.0\,\mathrm{km\cdot s^{-1}}$ and was transmitting information to it on the carrier frequency $f=2\,098\,\mathrm{MHz}$. What was the change of frequency $\Delta f$ between the oscillations transmitted by the module and the oscillations received by the Cassini probe, caused by the Doppler effect?

d) From the given data determine the mass of the planet Saturn $M_{\mathrm{Sat}}$ and the gravitational acceleration $a_{\mathrm{g}}$ at the surface of Titan.

Gravitational constant $G=6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2\cdot kg^{-2}}$, astronomical unit $1\,\mathrm{au}=1.50\cdot10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, mass of the Sun $M_{\mathrm{S}}=1.99\cdot10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$. The gravitational potential energy of a system of two bodies is given by $E_{\mathrm{p}}=-\dfrac{GmM}{r}$; the total energy of a body moving on an elliptical orbit with semi-major axis $a$ by $E=-\dfrac{GmM}{2a}$.

Note: In reality the Cassini–Huygens probe did not move along a Hohmann trajectory, but along a much more complicated trajectory using a multiple gravitational slingshot (gravity assist) method.

problems.title: Problem 4: Positron emission tomography (PET)
problems.problem:
Problem 4: Positron emission tomography (PET)

In this method the patient is given a radiopharmaceutical containing the nuclide $^{18}\mathrm{F}$ bound to glucose in the form of 2-deoxy-2-fluoro-D-glucose (FDG). The radionuclide $^{18}\mathrm{F}$ has a half-life $T=109.8\,\mathrm{min}$. The positron $\mathrm{e^+}$ produced in its transformation is practically stopped in the patient's tissue over a short path (a few mm) and annihilates with an electron $\mathrm{e^-}$. Both particles thereby disappear, and from the place of annihilation two photons $\gamma$, each with energy 511 keV, fly out simultaneously in opposite directions. In the simplest PET devices the photons are captured by a pair of detectors placed opposite each other (Fig. 3), which are connected by a circuit recording photons that arrived almost simultaneously. The circuit evaluates the time difference $\Delta t$ between the moments of arrival of the photons and determines the position of the place where the annihilation took place. From several thousand such captures a tomographic image of the examined person can then be created by a computer.

The nuclide $^{18}\mathrm{F}$ is prepared by bombarding atoms of oxygen $^{18}\mathrm{O}$ at rest with protons accelerated in a cyclotron to an energy of 4.00 MeV. In the accelerator there is a magnetic field of induction $B=1.0\,\mathrm{T}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/czech-2016-4-fig1.png

[Labels in the figure: pacient = patient, det. 1, det. 2 = detector 1, detector 2, Měřič časového rozdílu = time-difference meter, Obr. 3 = Fig. 3.]

a) Write the equation of the reaction for the preparation of the nuclide $^{18}\mathrm{F}$, determine the reaction energy $E_{\mathrm{r1}}$ in MeV and decide whether the reaction can take place at the given proton energy.

b) What speed do the protons acquire in the accelerator, and what is the maximum radius of their trajectory before they leave the cyclotron? In the solution you may use the relations of classical physics.

c) Write the equation of the $\beta^+$ decay of the nuclide $^{18}\mathrm{F}$, determine the reaction energy $E_{\mathrm{r2}}$ in MeV and verify that the reaction can take place spontaneously.

d) Explain why the photons produced by the annihilation of an electron and a positron fly off in mutually opposite directions and why each has an energy of 511 keV. Determine the wavelength $\lambda$ of these photons.

e) The time-difference meter between the signals from the detectors recorded at the second detector a time delay $\Delta t=0.70\,\mathrm{ns}$. Where was the place where the photons were produced?

f) The information for patients states that the radioactivity disappears by the next day. To what % of the original activity does the activity of the preparation drop in 24 hours?

In the solution use some of the following rest masses of particles and neutral atoms:

$m_{\mathrm{e}}=0.000\,549\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m_{\mathrm{p}}=1.007\,276\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m_{\mathrm{n}}=1.008\,665\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H})=1.007\,825\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H})=2.014\,102\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{16}_{8}\mathrm{O})=15.994\,915\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{17}_{8}\mathrm{O})=16.999\,132\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{18}_{8}\mathrm{O})=17.999\,161\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{17}_{9}\mathrm{F})=17.002\,095\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{18}_{9}\mathrm{F})=18.000\,938\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{19}_{9}\mathrm{F})=18.998\,403\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{18}_{10}\mathrm{Ne})=18.005\,708\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{19}_{10}\mathrm{Ne})=19.001\,880\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{20}\mathrm{Ne}_{10})=19.992\,440\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m(^{21}_{10}\mathrm{Ne})=20.993\,847\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$. Atomic mass constant $m_{\mathrm{u}}=1.66\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, speed of light in vacuum $c=3.00\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$, elementary charge $e=1.60\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

Problem 1: Radon 222

In the enclosed spaces of houses, radioactive radon and its decay products are present in the air. $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}$ is a member of the uranium–radium decay series, whose first member is $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$, and it decays with a half-life of 3.8 days to $^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}$. After the emission of the $\alpha$ particle the nucleus remains in its ground state. $^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}$ decays further with a half-life of 180 s. In this decay an $\alpha$ particle with kinetic energy 6.0 MeV is produced.

a) How many $\alpha$ decays and how many $\beta$ decays must occur for $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}$ to be formed from $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$? Write the decay equations of $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}$ and $^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}$.

b) Determine, in electronvolts, the energy $E_r$ released in the decay of $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}$.

Rest masses of the particles: $m\left(^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\right)=4.002\,603\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m\left(^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}\right)=222.017\,578\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$, $m\left(^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}\right)=218.008\,973\,m_{\mathrm{u}}$. Atomic mass constant $m_{\mathrm{u}}=1.660\,54\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

c) Determine the speed $v_\alpha$ of the $\alpha$ particle and the speed $v_{\mathrm{Po}}$ of the polonium nucleus after the decay of the $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}$ nucleus, assuming that the radon nucleus is at rest before the decay.

Problem 2: Free fall of a ball

At a distance $h=0.050\,\mathrm{m}$ below the ball there is an optical gate, and at a distance $s=1.000\,\mathrm{m}$ below it a second optical gate. The time measured between the passages through the optical gates was $t=0.362\,\mathrm{s}$.

a) Determine the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration $g$.

For a free fall of the ball from a greater height we must also consider the effect of the drag force, which depends on the square of the speed. Density of air $\rho_{vz}=1.29\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$, drag coefficient $C=0.48$, gravitational acceleration $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$.

b) Determine the maximum speed $v_{\max}$ with which the ball will fall in air.

c) How long a time $t_1$ will it take for the ball to reach the speed $v_1=30\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$, and what distance $s_1$ will it travel in that time?

problems.title: Problem 3: Jean Perrin's experiments
problems.problem:
Problem 3: Jean Perrin's experiments

Jean Perrin carried out experiments on the sedimentation of particles of gamboge (Czech: gumiguta), the milky sap of certain tropical plants, dispersed in water. He obtained particles of equal size by means of a centrifuge.

A spherical particle of radius $R=0.212\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ is in water of density $\rho_v=0.998\cdot10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$ at a distance $r=15.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the axis of a rotating centrifuge, which makes 2 500 revolutions per minute. Density of gamboge $\rho=1.194\cdot10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$, dynamic viscosity $\eta=1.005\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$. The flow of the liquid around the particles can be considered laminar.

a) Write the dependence of the speed $v$ of the radial motion of a gamboge particle on its distance $r$ from the axis of rotation, and determine its magnitude for a particle of radius $R$.

b) In what time $\tau$ does the distance of the particle from the axis increase by $l=5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$?

Onto the surface of water in a cylinder Perrin poured a thin layer of gamboge particles of the same radius $R=0.212\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ (obtained in the centrifuge).

c) With what speed $v_1$ will the particles sink towards the bottom of the vessel, and in what time $\tau_1$ will they travel the distance $l=5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$? The displacement caused by the Brownian motion of the particles can be neglected (as Einstein showed).

d) The dependence of air pressure on the height above the Earth's surface is given by the barometric equation:

$$p=p_0\,e^{-\frac{\rho_0 g\Delta h}{p_0}}.$$

Rearrange the barometric equation and determine for what change of height $\Delta h$, at a constant temperature $t=20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the number density of oxygen molecules in the atmosphere decreases by 1 %. Molar gas constant $R_m=8.31\,\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$, gravitational acceleration $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$. Molar mass of oxygen $M_m(\mathrm{O_2})=32\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

e) Perrin observed with a microscope the distribution of the density of particles of radius $R$ in water in the Earth's gravitational field at various temperatures. To a drop of emulsion containing a large number (about 13 000) of particles he added water, covered it with a cover glass, turned it on its side, and after equilibrium had been established he observed with the microscope from the side the decrease of the number of particles in the upward direction.

A theoretical analysis (A. Einstein) showed that the particles of the emulsion behave in the same way as an ideal gas, and their number density decreases with height similarly to the number density of oxygen molecules in the gravitational field in the atmosphere. Perrin then counted the particles directly. The results for the temperature $t=20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are in the following table:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} \text{Height} & 5\,\mathrm{\mu m} & 35\,\mathrm{\mu m} & 65\,\mathrm{\mu m} & 95\,\mathrm{\mu m} \\ \hline \text{Concentration} & 100 & 47 & 22.6 & 12 \end{array}$$

From these data estimate, to one significant figure (as Perrin did), the value of the Avogadro constant $N_{\mathrm{A}}$.

Problem 1: The Curiosity probe

In August 2012 a probe landed on Mars with the self-propelled rover Curiosity, used for exploring the surface of Mars. The rover is powered by a radioisotope generator based on the radioactive $\alpha$-decay of ${}^{238}_{94}\mathrm{Pu}$. The heat released in the decay is converted into electrical energy by thermocouples with an efficiency of $6.0\,\%$.

a) Write the equation of the $\alpha$-decay of ${}^{238}_{94}\mathrm{Pu}$ and determine the heat $Q$ released in one decay. Let us assume that all the energy is released in the form of heat.

b) What must the initial mass of ${}^{238}_{94}\mathrm{Pu}$ be if the initial thermal power $P_0$ is planned to be $2.00\,\mathrm{kW}$?

Problem 3: Charge transfer

Two identical conducting spheres A and B of radius $R$ carry charges of the same sign $Q_{\mathrm{A}0}$ and $Q_{\mathrm{B}0}$, respectively. We will transfer charge by means of a small, conducting, initially uncharged ball of radius $r$, in such a way that we first touch sphere A, then sphere B and then sphere A again. Let $Q_{\mathrm{A}k}$ and $Q_{\mathrm{B}k}$ denote the charges of the spheres after the $k$-th transfer. By one transfer we mean touching sphere B with the charged ball and the subsequent touching of sphere A

a) Let there be a charge $Q$ on a sphere of radius $R$. After contact, the small ball of radius $r$ will carry the charge $q = \gamma Q$. Determine in general the coefficient $\gamma$, which we will consider known from now on.

b) Determine the charges of the spheres $Q_{\mathrm{A}k}$ and $Q_{\mathrm{B}k}$ after the $k$-th transfer of charge. Solve first in general, then for the values $Q_{\mathrm{A}0} = 10.0\,\mathrm{nC}$, $Q_{\mathrm{B}0} = 1.0\,\mathrm{nC}$, $\gamma = 0.02$ and $k = 10$. a) How long a time $\tau_1$ will it take to heat the water to the boiling point?

b) How long a time $\tau_2$ from the beginning of the experiment will it take until all the water has evaporated?

c) What will the temperature in the vessel be at the time $\tau_3 = 2.5\,\mathrm{h}$ after the beginning of the experiment, and what will the volume of the vapour in the vessel be?

problems.title: Problem 3: The Mössbauer effect
problems.problem:
Problem 3: The Mössbauer effect

Under normal conditions, the emission of a gamma quantum is accompanied by a recoil of the atomic nucleus. The energy (frequency) of the emitted radiation changes according to the magnitude of the recoil. At low temperatures the nucleus becomes so firmly a part of the crystal lattice that the lattice absorbs the recoil energy. The energy of the emitted gamma quantum can then be determined as the difference between the energies of the excited and the ground state of the nucleus and is therefore well defined. This effect was discovered by the German physicist Rudolf Ludwig Mössbauer, born in 1929, who received the Nobel Prize for this discovery in 1961.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/czech-2020-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1a), Fig. 1b)

a) A rifle of mass $M$ is propped against a fixed wall. When it is fired, the bullet leaves the barrel of the rifle with a speed of magnitude $v_0$ (Fig. 1a). The ratio of the masses of the bullet and the rifle is $\mu = \frac{m}{M}$. The energy $E_0$ supplied by the burnt gases, released at each shot, is independent of the motion of the rifle and is equal to the kinetic energy of the bullet relative to the rifle.

What would the speed $v$ of the bullet be if the rifle were not propped against the wall but could move freely (Fig. 1b)?

Find the relative change of the speed of the bullet $\dfrac{\Delta v}{v_0} = \dfrac{v - v_0}{v_0}$ assuming that the mass of the bullet is negligible compared with the mass of the rifle ($\mu \to 0$).

Find the relative change of the energy of the bullet $\dfrac{\Delta E}{E_0} = \dfrac{E - E_0}{E_0}$ assuming that the mass of the bullet is negligible compared with the mass of the rifle ($\mu \to 0$).

You may use the relations $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}} \approx 1 - \dfrac{1}{2}x$, $\dfrac{1}{1-x} \approx 1 + x$.

b) An excited atomic nucleus of mass $M$ at a very low temperature (the nucleus is an almost motionless part of the crystal lattice) emits a photon of $\gamma$ radiation of energy $hf_0$. An excited nucleus at ordinary temperature (it can be regarded as free, able to recoil) emits a photon of energy $hf$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/czech-2020-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2

Determine the ratio

$$\frac{\Delta\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\varepsilon - \varepsilon_0}{\varepsilon_0}, \quad \text{where } \varepsilon = \frac{hf}{Mc^2} \text{ and } \varepsilon_0 = \frac{hf_0}{Mc^2}.$$

Solve the problem classically (without considering the rest energy) and relativistically (taking the rest energy into account), and compare the relations for negligibly small $\varepsilon_0$ ($\varepsilon_0 \to 0$). In relativistic physics the relation between energy and mass is $E^2 = M^2c^4 + p^2c^2$.

c) Mössbauer used nuclei of iridium ${}^{191}_{77}\mathrm{Ir}$ emitting, in the fixed state, quanta of energy $E_0 = 129\,\mathrm{keV}$. Determine the approximate rest energy of the iridium nucleus (do not take the mass defect into account), the parameter $\varepsilon_0$ and the speed $u$ of the free iridium nucleus after the emission of the quantum. Mass of the proton and of the neutron $m_p \cong m_n = 1.7\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, speed of light $c = 3.0\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$, elementary charge $e = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.

What is the ratio $\dfrac{\Delta\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}$ for the $\gamma$ photons leaving the nucleus in this case? Solve the problem using the classical result of part b).

d) A gamma photon emitted by a free iridium nucleus can hit another free iridium nucleus in the ground state and might be absorbed in it. The energy of the photon, however, is reduced by the recoil, and on absorption by a free nucleus a further part of the energy would be converted into motion of the nucleus, and only the remaining energy of the photon could cause the excitation of the nucleus. A so-called resonance would then arise between the two nuclei. For a resonance to arise, however, the energy (frequency) of the photon is already too small. To achieve resonance, Mössbauer decided to use the Doppler effect to increase the frequency of the photons.

With what relative speed did the source of the $\gamma$ quanta have to move towards the receiver, which also contained free ${}^{191}_{77}\mathrm{Ir}$ nuclei, for resonance to occur? For the change of frequency when the source moves towards the receiver, the following holds:

$$\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} \approx \frac{v_0}{c}.$$

problems.title: Problem 2: Speed measurement by radar

Problem 2: Speed measurement by radar

On a straight road a driver drives at a constant speed $v$ and behind him a police car drives at a constant speed $u$. The police car is equipped with a radar which emits electromagnetic waves of frequency $f_0$ in the direction of the car in front of it and at the same time registers the reflected waves. The speeds of both cars are negligible compared with the speed $c$ of propagation of electromagnetic waves.

a) Determine the frequency $f_1$ with which the waves are reflected from the observed car, and the frequency $f_2$ with which these waves are registered by the radar in the police car. Show that the relative change of frequency $|f_0-f_2|/f_0$ of the waves emitted and received by the radar is, in the first-order approximation in the quantities $v/c$ and $u/c$, directly proportional to the difference of the speeds $|v-u|$.

b) Real speed measurement is based on the fact that when two waves of close frequencies are superposed, beats arise, from whose period the relative speed of the cars $|v-u|$ can be determined. Determine the period of the beats $T_r$ as a function of the relative speed of the vehicles, first in general, then for the numerical values $f_0=1.50\,\mathrm{GHz}$ and $|v-u|=10\,\mathrm{km\cdot h^{-1}}$.

Solve the problem without using relativistic relations. Adjust the expressions obtained so that, to first-order accuracy, they are linear in the variables $v/c$ and $u/c$. For small quantities $x$, $|x|\ll1$, the relation $(1+x)^s\approx1+sx$ holds to first-order accuracy in $x$, where $s$ is a real number. You may use the formula $\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=2\cos\dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\cos\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$ or $\sin\alpha+\sin\beta=2\cos\dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\sin\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$.

We define the concentration as the ratio $w=\dfrac{m_s}{m_{\mathrm{roztoku}}}$, where $m_s$ is the mass of the salt [$m_{\mathrm{roztoku}}$ = mass of the solution].

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \dfrac{m_s}{\mathrm{g}} & 10 & 50 & 100 & 200 & 350 \\ \hline \dfrac{q}{\mathrm{kJ\cdot kg^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}} & 72.3 & 66.2 & 57.3 & 42.5 & 32.2 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

problems.title: Problem 1: Air conditioning of a room
problems.problem:
Problem 1: Air conditioning of a room

The air conditioning of a room can be described as a heat engine working in the reverse mode: it takes heat $Q_{\mathrm{m}}$ from the room at temperature $T_{\mathrm{m}}$ and gives off heat $Q_{\mathrm{v}}>Q_{\mathrm{m}}$ to the air around the house at temperature $T_{\mathrm{v}}$. The electric compressor must supply work $W$ in doing so. Let us assume that the device works as a Carnot engine with the maximum possible efficiency.

a) The electrical part of the device works with power $P$. What amount of heat $Q_{\mathrm{m}}$ does it remove from the room in time $\Delta t$?

b) Even when the room is insulated, heat enters it from outside at the rate $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}=k\Delta T$, where $\Delta T=T_{\mathrm{v}}-T_{\mathrm{m}}$ is the temperature difference between the surroundings of the house and the room and $k$ is a constant. To what lowest temperature can the temperature of the air in the room be reduced for a given temperature of the outside air $T_{\mathrm{v}}$, a given power $P$ and a given value of the constant $k$? Express the result in terms of these three quantities.

c) What minimum power $P$ of the air conditioning do we need if we want to keep the temperature $t_{\mathrm{m}}=25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in the room at an outside temperature $t_{\mathrm{v}}=40\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, if the usual value of the constant is $k=173\,\mathrm{W\cdot K^{-1}}$?

a) In what ratio are the masses $m_1$, $m_2$, the radii $r_1$, $r_2$ and the charges $Q_1$, $Q_2$?

Problem 3: Diffraction and interference of neutrons

The neutrons from the source have speed $2.7\,\mathrm{km\cdot s^{-1}}$.

In the interference pattern the distance between the 3rd-order maxima was then measured to be $440\,\mathrm{\mu m}$. What speed of the neutrons does this correspond to?

Problem 4: Zoom lens (transfocator)

A frequently used function of cameras is the change of the focal length of the lens, which makes it possible to bring an object closer or move it further away. For this purpose an optical transfocator (also known as a zoom) is used. Its principle lies in changing the angular magnification of the lens.

Fig. 4 shows a simplified scheme of an ordinary objective with a converging lens, which projects the rays from a distant object onto the surface of the recording medium (you solved such a case in the regional round). The maximum field angle $\varphi_0$ is the larger, the smaller the focal length $f_0$ of the lens.

A simple transfocator (Fig. 5) consists of two converging lenses $\mathrm{S}_1$, $\mathrm{S}_2$ and a diverging lens $\mathrm{R}$. The mutual distance $d$ of the converging lenses is fixed; the diverging lens can be moved between the converging lenses. As the position $x$ of the diverging lens is changed smoothly, the focal length of the objective changes continuously. The lenses are chosen so that a beam of parallel rays entering at the angle $\varphi_1$ leaves the transfocator as a beam of parallel rays at the angle $\varphi_0$, with no change in the orientation of the angle between the beam of rays and the optical axis, as can be seen in the figure.

Consider converging lenses $\mathrm{S}_1$ and $\mathrm{S}_2$ with focal lengths $f_1$, $f_2$ and a diverging lens $\mathrm{R}$ with focal length $f_3<0$. The extreme positions of the diverging lens $\mathrm{R}$ are either at the lens $\mathrm{S}_1$ (in that case $x=0$) or at the lens $\mathrm{S}_2$ ($x=d$). When the diverging lens is moved between these positions we require the field angle $\varphi_1$ to change in the ratio $\dfrac{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_{1,\max}}{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_{1,\min}}=n$ (at the same output angle $\varphi_0$).

a) The diverging lens $\mathrm{R}$ is moved right up to the converging lens $\mathrm{S}_1$ ($x=0$). Determine the focal length $f_4$ of the system $\mathrm{S}_1$-$\mathrm{R}$. At the distance $d$ from the assembly $\mathrm{S}_1$-$\mathrm{R}$ draw the converging lens $\mathrm{S}_2$ so that the beam of incident parallel rays leaves the system again as a beam of parallel rays and so that both beams make equally oriented angles with the optical axis (both oriented in the same way, clockwise or anticlockwise). Show graphically the passage of the rays through this system and state the conditions that the quantities $f_1$, $f_2$, $f_3$ must satisfy. Then express in general the ratio $\dfrac{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_1}{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_0}$, where $\varphi_1$ is the angle at which the beam of rays enters the system and $\varphi_0$ is the angle at which the beam leaves the system.

b) In the second case the diverging lens $\mathrm{R}$ is moved right up to the converging lens $\mathrm{S}_2$ ($x=d$). Determine the focal length $f_5$ of the system $\mathrm{R}$-$\mathrm{S}_2$. In front of the assembly $\mathrm{R}$-$\mathrm{S}_2$, at the distance $d$, draw the converging lens $\mathrm{S}_1$ so that the beam of parallel rays incident on the lens $\mathrm{S}_1$ leaves the system again as a beam of parallel rays, and so that both beams make equally oriented angles with the optical axis. Show graphically the passage of the rays through this system and state the conditions that the quantities $f_1$, $f_2$, $f_3$ must satisfy. Express in general the ratio $\dfrac{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi'_1}{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_0}$, where $\varphi'_1$ is the angle at which the beam of rays enters the system and $\varphi_0$ is the angle at which the beam leaves the system.

c) For both extreme positions of the diverging lens $\mathrm{R}$ in the transfocator the distance $d$ is the same, and the output angle $\varphi_0$ is also the same. Determine the focal lengths $f_1$, $f_2$, $f_3$ of the lenses so that for the input angles $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi'_1$

$$\frac{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_{1,\max}}{\mathrm{tg}\,\varphi_{1,\min}}=n,$$

where $n>1$ is a given number. Solve in general and then for the values $d=4.0\,\mathrm{cm}$, $n=3$.

Assume that all lenses are thin. Hint: When lenses are placed close together, their optical power is equal to the sum of the optical powers of the lenses.

Problem 1: Mission to Mars

One of the possible ways in which future crewed missions to Mars could proceed is that the spacecraft will fly from the orbit of the Earth to the orbit of Mars along an elliptical transfer trajectory that touches both planetary orbits tangentially. The perihelion of this trajectory is on the orbit of the Earth and the aphelion on the orbit of Mars. Despite some disadvantages, this trajectory is commonly used in interplanetary flights because it is relatively economical. In this problem you will investigate some properties of this trajectory.

a) Determine the orbital period of Mars $T_M$, i.e. the length of the Martian year.

b) Determine the time $t$ of a one-way flight to Mars along such a trajectory.

c) The spacecraft is placed on this trajectory by a short but powerful firing of the engine near the Earth (because it is more efficient to burn the fuel in a quick impulse while the spacecraft is still near the Earth). How large a change of velocity $\Delta v_1$ is needed for the spacecraft near the Earth to pass onto the transfer orbit? Neglect atmospheric drag and assume that near the Earth the spacecraft moves together with it, i.e. it has the same velocity relative to the Sun as the Earth.

d) Estimate the change of velocity $\Delta v_2$ needed to enter an almost circular orbit near Mars.

The mean distance of Mars from the Sun is $r_M=1.52\,\mathrm{au}$, the mean distance of the Earth is $r_Z=1.00\,\mathrm{au}=1.50\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{km}$. The mass of the Sun is $M_S=1.99\cdot10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

problems.title: Problem 2: Magnetic buffer

Problem 2: Magnetic buffer

An elastic mechanical buffer, e.g. on railway wagons, contains a spring that is compressed in a collision and thereby absorbs the kinetic energy of the wagon. After the wagon collides with a stationary obstacle, the deceleration of the wagon when an elastic buffer is used is substantially smaller than it would be in a hard (inelastic) collision, and so we can prevent mechanical damage to the wagon. A magnetic buffer could work in a similar way.

Let us consider the following model of the buffer: along horizontal electrically conducting rails, whose mutual distance is $l$, a trolley moves which represents a perfect electrical short circuit. To simplify the model, instead of a real wagon we consider a conducting rod of mass $m$ on wheels, which rolls along the rails with very small friction. At the end of the rails a coil of inductance $L$ is wound. The end part of the track is in a uniform magnetic field of induction of magnitude $B$, whose vector points vertically upwards. The trolley moves perpendicular to this magnetic field, and as soon as it enters it, it starts to decelerate as a result of the action of the current in the coil and the magnetic field.

a) Draw an illustrative figure and mark the necessary quantities in it. Briefly describe the physical nature of the process that takes place after the trolley enters the magnetic field. Explain why the trolley starts to decelerate practically immediately after entering the magnetic field.

b) The trolley, the rails and the coil form a closed electric circuit with very small resistance. Derive an expression for the current $i$ in this circuit as a function of time and verify by direct substitution that the general solution indeed has the form

$$i(t)=I_0+I_m\sin\left(\omega t+\alpha\right).$$

Also determine the individual parameters of this solution: $I_0$, $I_m$, $\omega$, $\alpha$.

c) Determine the dependence of the velocity of the trolley $v(t)$ on time and determine the time $\tau$ that elapses from the moment the trolley enters the magnetic field until it stops.

d) Determine the magnitude of the stiffness of the magnetic spring $k=\dfrac{F}{x}$.

Solve first in general, then for the values $m=50\,\mathrm{g}$, $l=20\,\mathrm{cm}$, $L=1.5\,\mathrm{H}$, $B=1.0\,\mathrm{T}$, $v_0=60\,\mathrm{cm\cdot s^{-1}}$.

Hint: The derivative of the function $f(t)=a+b\sin\left(ct+d\right)$ with respect to time is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}f(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=bc\cos(ct+d),$$

the derivative of the function $g(t)=a+b\cos(ct+d)$ with respect to time is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}g(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=-bc\sin(ct+d),$$

and further

$$\int_0^t\cos c\vartheta\,\mathrm{d}\vartheta=\frac{1}{c}\sin c\,t.$$

problems.title: Problem 3: Bungee jumping

Problem 3: Bungee jumping

In this adrenaline sport a person of mass $m=70\,\mathrm{kg}$ jumps from a platform that is at a height $h=90\,\mathrm{m}$ above a lake. A rubber rope of length $L$ and stiffness $k$ is attached to the jumper's feet; the other end of the rope is firmly fixed to the platform. Near the water surface the jumper must have zero velocity and acceleration $a_0=2g$. Let us assume that the deformation of the rope obeys Hooke's law. Neglect the dimensions of the jumper, the mass of the rope, air resistance and conversions of energy in the rope into forms other than elastic potential energy.

Under these conditions determine:

a) the length $L$ of the unstretched rope and its stiffness $k$,

b) the length of the rope in the equilibrium position,

c) the maximum speed of the person $v_{\max}$,

d) the time $t$ in which the person reaches the water surface.

Caution! The accuracy of your calculations may be crucial for the safety of the jumper!

problems.title: Problem 4: Standard atmosphere
problems.problem:
Problem 4: Standard atmosphere

Since neither the isothermal nor the adiabatic atmosphere is an ideal model, in practice the so-called standard model of the atmosphere (International Standard Atmosphere, ISA) is often used. The ISA model does not take into account variations in place and time and assigns to each altitude one value of density, pressure and temperature. This allows us, for example, to calibrate pressure-based instruments (altimeter, airspeed indicator, variometer) in a uniform way. A constant composition of the atmosphere and the validity of the ideal-gas laws are assumed. In describing the atmosphere we shall use physical constants valid to the stated precision, whose values are:

Molar mass of air $M_m=28.96\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

Molar gas constant $R=8.314\,\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$.

Gravitational acceleration $g=9.807\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$.

Atmospheric pressure at sea level $p_0=1.013\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

Air temperature at sea level $t_0=15.00\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Temperature of absolute zero $t_{an}=-273.15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Up to the altitude $z=11.0\,\mathrm{km}$ the air temperature decreases linearly by $\dfrac{\Delta t}{\Delta z}=6.500\,\dfrac{^{\circ}\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{km}}$, i.e. by $6.500\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for every kilometre of altitude.

a) Calculate the density of air at sea level $\rho_0$.

b) Write the relation for the dependence of the thermodynamic temperature $T$ on the altitude $z$ in the form

$$T(z)=T_0\left(1-\frac{z}{h}\right)$$

and determine the numerical values of the parameters $T_0$ and $h$.

c) Derive the relation for the changes of atmospheric pressure with altitude $\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta z}$ for small changes $\Delta z$.

d) The relations for the atmospheric pressure and density in the ISA model have the form $p(z)=p_0\left(1-\dfrac{z}{h}\right)^{\alpha}$ and $\rho(z)=\rho_0\left(1-\dfrac{z}{h}\right)^{\beta}$. Determine the numerical values of the constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

Problem 1: Ball game

A boy stood at a distance $d=6.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from a high vertical wall and kicked a ball at the wall. At the upper edge of the wall, at a height $h=7.5\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground, there was a rain gutter (Fig. 1). The boy's father warned him not to kick the ball too high, because if it fell into the gutter, it would be a problem to get the ball out. On a horizontal playing field the boy kicked the same ball to a maximum distance $D=14\,\mathrm{m}$.

a) Draw a picture of the trajectory of the ball when kicked on the horizontal playing field and mark the necessary quantities in it. Derive the equation of the vertical coordinate $y$ of the trajectory of the ball as a function of the horizontal coordinate $x$ and the parameters $v_0$, $\alpha$.

b) Determine the value $v_{0\,\mathrm{max}}$ of the initial speed $v_0$ of the ball that the boy is able to give to the ball.

c) Verify by calculation whether the boy is able, from the distance $d$ in front of the wall, to kick the ball into the gutter if he uses his maximum kick speed $v_{0\,\mathrm{max}}$. If the answer is positive, determine the angle $\alpha$ at which the ball must be kicked.

d) Determine theoretically the minimum value $v_{0\,\mathrm{min}}$ of the initial speed $v_0$ of the ball for the boy to kick the ball into the gutter from the distance $d$ from the wall.

Do not take into account the height of the boy or the dimensions of the gutter, i.e. the ball is kicked from the level $h_0=0$ and the point where it lands in the gutter is at the horizontal distance $d$ from the place of the kick. Neglect air resistance, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$.

problems.title: Problem 2: Thermal process

Problem 2: Thermal process

Nitrogen of amount of substance $n=1.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ is enclosed by a piston in a cylinder. The initial volume of the gas is $V_1=20.0\,\mathrm{l}$. First we compress the gas with the piston from the initial volume $V_1$ to half the volume, $V_2$, at constant temperature $T_1=400\,\mathrm{K}$; then, in the second phase of the process, we heat the gas to the temperature $T_2=700\,\mathrm{K}$ at constant volume $V_2$. In the third phase of the process the gas expands to the original volume $V_1$ at constant temperature $T_2$, and in the fourth phase the gas returns to the initial state at constant volume.

a) Determine the values of the pressure in the individual states of transition between the phases of the process and represent the process graphically in a $pV$-diagram.

b) Determine the efficiency $\eta$ of the process.

Consider a Carnot cycle that has the first phase in common with the original process, while the second and fourth phases are replaced by adiabatic processes. The temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ of the isothermal phases remain the same as in the original cycle.

c) Determine the initial volume $V_3$ and the final volume $V_4$ of the third phase of the Carnot cycle and draw this cycle with a dashed line in the graph of the original process.

d) Determine the efficiency $\eta_C$ of the Carnot cycle with the temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ and find the ratio $\frac{\eta_C}{\eta}$.

Solve the problem in general and then for the given numerical values. The molar gas constant is $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}}$, the Poisson constant (adiabatic index) of nitrogen is $\kappa=1.40$. Treat the gas as ideal.

Note: The molar heat capacity of an ideal gas at constant volume is

$$C_V=\frac{R}{\kappa-1}.$$

Hint: The work in an isothermal process between states $A$ and $B$ is

$$W_{AB}=\int_{V_A}^{V_B}p\,\mathrm{d}V.$$

Problem 3: Electromagnetic brake

Electromagnetic brakes are used for braking large vehicles, for example high-speed trains. Instead of the power supply, a resistor is connected to the motor, so that the motor works as a generator of electric current and the electrical energy is converted into heat in the resistor.

We shall use a simple model of a rectangular coil of area $S$, with $N$ turns and with resistance $R_z$, which rotates in a constant and uniform magnetic field of magnetic induction $B$ (see Figure 2). A resistor of resistance $R$ is connected to the coil by means of sliding contacts. At the beginning, at the moment the resistor is connected, the coil rotates with angular velocity $\omega_0$.

a) Determine the amplitude $I_m$ of the current flowing through the resistor of resistance $R$ at the angular velocity $\omega_0$.

b) Determine the mean value $P$ of the thermal power released in the coil–resistor system. Further determine the value $P_0$ of this power at the angular velocity $\omega_0$.

c) Determine the braking torque $M$ acting on the rotating coil at angular velocity $\omega$, and the value $M_0$ of this torque at the angular velocity $\omega_0$.

d) Determine after how many revolutions $n$ the coil stops as a result of the electromagnetic braking, if the moment of inertia of the rotating part is $J$.

Problem 4: The Y-12 Complex

During the Manhattan Project it was necessary to obtain a large quantity of the uranium isotope 235. In the facility code-named the Y-12 Complex there were in total 1152 devices known as calutrons (an acronym from CALifornia University cycloTRON). These were mass spectrometers in which ionized gas was accelerated by a voltage $U$ and then bent in a uniform magnetic field of induction $\boldsymbol{B}$ ($\boldsymbol{v}\perp\boldsymbol{B}$) so that it fell into collecting vessels (collectors, Fig. 3). The uniform magnetic field fills the region $y>0$; the line $y=0$ is its boundary. Since the difference between the masses of the isotopes $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ is very small, the accuracy of the aiming of the ion beam was crucial.

a) Let us first assume that all ions leave the source at the point $(0,0)$ exactly in the direction of the $y$ axis (perpendicular to the boundary of the magnetic field). Derive an expression for the radius $R$ of the trajectory of an ion of mass $m$ and charge $+q_e$. Determine the distance $d$ between the points of impact (the intersections of the paths with the line $y=0$) for the isotopes $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$.

b) Show that the time of flight of the ions during the bending through $180^\circ$ in the uniform field does not depend on $U$. Calculate the difference of the times of impact of two ions that were emitted simultaneously: $\Delta t=t_{238}-t_{235}$.

c) In a real source the ions leave the source with an angular spread. Let a $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ ion leave the origin at an angle $\alpha$ from the $y$ axis (where $\alpha=0$ is the ideal perpendicular direction). The coordinate $x$ where the ion, after describing a semicircle, lands back on the plane $y=0$ is given by the relation:

$$x(\alpha)=2R\cos\alpha. \qquad (1)$$

For small angles $\alpha$ (where $\cos\alpha\approx1-\alpha^2/2$ holds) determine the total width $\Delta x$ of the trace of the beam if the angles $\alpha$ range over the interval $\langle-\alpha_{\max},\alpha_{\max}\rangle$.

d) Derive formula (1).
